appraisal_events.evidence: je venais d'adresser à Albertine les paroles les plus dures et les plus humiliantes... quelques larmes que je remarquai sans paraître les voir, mais non sans en être réjoui
appraisal_events.explanation: In this staged scene the narrator deliberately humiliates Albertine and takes secret pleasure in her tears, reversing what Rosemonde recalls as her former favor ('elle n'est plus bonne à donner à manger aux chiens'); this positions le narrateur as gaining emotional leverage while Albertine is locally diminished.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Ah ! c'est sûrement la série dont nous a parlé Elstir, le plus grand des peintres contemporains, s'écria Albertine qui n'avait rien dit jusque-là. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Albertine breaks her silence to praise Elstir emphatically as the greatest contemporary painter, a genuine local admiration event.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Vous me permettrez de lui préférer Le Sidaner, Mademoiselle »... « il a gâché sa vie. » Mme de Cambremer donna raison à l'avocat en ce qui concernait Elstir.
appraisal_events.explanation: The avocat dismisses Elstir in favor of the minor painter Le Sidaner and Mme de Cambremer endorses this verdict, but the passage frames both judges as pretentious dilettantes, so the discredit of Elstir is locally undercut by narratorial irony.

status_effects.explanation: Albertine is openly humiliated and reduced to tears by the narrator in this staged moment, a sharp local reversal from her previously favored status.

As in-scene participant, the narrator stages his own dominance over Albertine, deliberately wounding her and privately relishing her distress, which locally elevates his emotional leverage in the relationship.
Albertine's spontaneous, emphatic praise locally raises Elstir's esteem.
The avocat's and Mme de Cambremer's dismissive verdict locally lowers Elstir's esteem, though the irony surrounding these judges' own taste tempers the force of this diminishment.
